description: We are a two-person team from Taiwan. One of us works in financial IT as a business analyst with a software engineering background (Python, SQL, system design, testing). The other develops robot vision and image recognition at a robotics company. We want to build a practical, working solution for this challenge.
summary:
Can radar tell us how much water is left? Taiwan's Water Pulse is an interactive web app that follows four Taiwanese reservoirs through a year of retreat and recovery, using NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar and official Taiwan Water Resources Agency observations.

It tracks and visualizes one surface change, reservoir water shrinking and refilling, through date comparison, a timeline and charts. In two reservoirs, radar area tracked official water levels (Pearson r = 0.94 and 0.91). For those two, the app reports only "High" at high storage, with finer levels unresolved; at low water it estimates storage and shows the observed errors (Baoshan II: mean 5.2, maximum 9.2 percentage points).

Built on historical observations and exploratory estimates, not live monitoring, Taiwan's Water Pulse makes reservoir change visible: a useful reference tool.
details:
Taiwan’s Water Pulse: can radar tell us how much water is left?

What it does

Taiwan’s Water Pulse is an interactive web workspace that follows four Taiwanese reservoirs (Baoshan II, Liyutan, Shimen and Feitsui) through a year of retreat and recovery, November 2025 to October 2026, as seen by NISAR L-band radar. Radar passes are paired with the official gauge reading taken the same morning by Taiwan’s Water Resources Agency (WRA), so users can see what radar captures, what it misses, and how far a radar-based storage estimate can be trusted. It is a historical archive, not live monitoring or a forecast.

How it works

  1. Observe. Each reservoir has 21 NISAR GCOV acquisitions (HH and HV) across 30 twelve-day slots. The nine slots with no product, including a 95-day gap from March to June 2026, stay empty. Nothing is interpolated.
  2. Map water. HH power is averaged onto a 30 m grid. Inside the OpenStreetMap reservoir outline, pixels below 60% of that date’s surrounding-land median count as candidate water. Gauge data evaluate this rule but never tune it.
  3. Grade. The same method runs on all four reservoirs. Each gets a grade from how closely radar area follows the official water level (Pearson r with a 95% confidence interval) and whether the change exceeds the method’s own threshold sensitivity.
  4. Estimate. Only A-grade reservoirs get a storage estimate, in two stages. While radar area is within its full-pool range, the app reports “High; finer levels unresolved”. Once the water recedes, it gives a calibrated percentage with a descriptive error range.
  5. Explore. Users compare any two dates with a swipe or side-by-side view, play the timeline, add official water level, CWA station rainfall and recorded events to the charts, move the classification threshold themselves, and trace each observation to its NISAR product ID. The interface runs in English and Traditional Chinese on desktop and mobile, with a 30-second guided tour.

What a year of data showed

  • Radar area tracked the official water level in two reservoirs: Baoshan II (r = 0.94) and Liyutan (r = 0.91), both grade A. Feitsui’s change was smaller than the method’s sensitivity (grade B). Shimen’s change could not be resolved (grade C), so its area values are withheld.
  • Surface area is not stored volume. Between 6 November 2025 and 18 March 2026, official storage at Baoshan II (Hsinchu) fell from 100.0% to 28.2% and the water level dropped 20.56 m, while the radar-visible surface shrank only 11.5%.
  • Radar becomes more useful as water recedes. Above roughly 68–71% storage it could only say “High”. At low water, leave-one-out estimates missed by 5.2 percentage points on average for Baoshan II and 4.0 for Liyutan, with a largest miss of 10.4. One full-pool date was misclassified as low.
  • Radar missed the lowest point. Baoshan II’s lowest sampled gauge reading, 22.4% on 31 March 2026, fell inside the 95-day gap.

Benefits and intended impact

Reservoir storage in Taiwan swings between dry winters and rainy-season refills, and the public follows it closely. L-band radar sees through cloud and at night, so it can observe reservoirs when optical satellites cannot. But seeing a water surface is not the same as knowing how much water is stored. Taiwan’s Water Pulse gives students, journalists and the public a local, concrete way to read SAR imagery, and gives practitioners a transparent check on whether a reservoir has a usable radar signal before anyone relies on an estimate. Radar cannot replace a gauge, so we position the project as a reference tool. Because the pipeline and evaluation are reproducible, the same method can be rerun as NISAR’s archive grows: first on a second drawdown, then where current gauge data are not available.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data pipeline: Python 3.14 with uv; earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj and rasterio; pytest and Ruff.
  • Web app: TypeScript, React 19 and Vite. Radar frames are drawn on HTML Canvas and charts are hand-built in SVG, with no mapping or charting library. Tested with Vitest and deployed as a static site on Vercel.
  • Data: NISAR L-band GCOV (NASA/JPL and ISRO, distributed by ASF DAAC), WRA reservoir observations, Central Weather Administration (CWA) station rainfall, and OpenStreetMap outlines.
  • AI/SI tools: OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude assisted with analysis, code, tests, interface copy, translation, documentation, data preparation and the demo video. The video narration is synthetic speech generated with Kokoro. All radar and gauge observations are real, and no scientific imagery is generated.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. Everything was built on personal computers, and the site runs in any modern browser.
  • License: MIT for the code.

What makes it creative

  • Limits are part of the design. No clear signal means no number: Shimen’s area is withheld, high water is reported only as “High”, the radar gap stays blank, and error bars show the errors we observed instead of a promised accuracy. An earlier method that failed its held-out test is still published.
  • It is a report card, not a success story: one method, four reservoirs, two it can follow and two it cannot.
  • Users can change the threshold and watch the answer move, so they can test for themselves how sensitive the result is.
  • Results can be traced and recomputed, with product IDs, UTC and Taiwan timestamps, CSV downloads, and an evaluation that reruns offline from the published files.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific validity. Correlation is not causation. The 60% threshold is a chosen definition, so we show how results change between 50% and 70%. Quality-flagged passes are kept and marked. A volume-closure check for Baoshan II (25.74 vs 24.28 million m³) is presented as a consistency check, not independent validation.
  • Data limits. NISAR products are provisional, the archive holds 21 passes and a single drawdown, and the radar pass (about 05:16) precedes the 07:00 gauge reading by 1.7 hours. All results are exploratory.
  • Hypotheses, labelled as such. HH area fell 11.5% while HV fell only 2.9%. Exposed reservoir bed may stay dark in HV, but we have no ground observations to confirm this. Rainfall and event layers are context, not proof of cause.
  • Audience and access. Plain-language labels, two languages, light and dark themes, keyboard shortcuts and a mobile layout.
  • Openness and safety. A static site with no backend and no credentials, version-controlled published data, attribution for every source, and no agency logos or implied endorsement.
